newsitem.title: USA: Stocks end winning streak, bonds firmer on data.
newsitem.headline: Stocks end winning streak, bonds firmer on data.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks fell on Thursday, ending a three-session rally that had added nearly 290 points to the Dow Jones industrial average, but bonds rose on downbeat economic data.
The dollar was mixed.

The Dow Jones industrial average ended 21.27 points lower at 6,658.60. In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,295 to 1,185 on active volume of 502 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Dow's performance since Monday was paralleled in recent history only by a 289-point surge in the two days after the "Black Monday" market crash of 1987.
"The market seemed a little tired today," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd.
Once again, the market turned in a mixed performance, but this time it was technology shares that rallied as blue chips fell victim to profit-taking.
"Techs had dramatically lagged and today it was like someone finally said it was O.K. to buy techs," said Peter Coolidge, senior equity trader at Brean Murray & Co.
Analysts said much of the buying in technology and other sectors appeared focused on the top tier names, which they said was evidence the market remained on edge.
"This rally has been as narrow as any we've seen this year," Bleier said. "The money coming in is seeking out the very top names."
A strong bond market boosted interest-rate-sensitive sectors like transportation and finance.
The 30-year Treasury bond rose 12/32, or $3.75 on a $1,000 bond, lowering its yield to 7.07 percent from Wednesday's close of 7.10 percent. The price and yield move in opposite directions.
Bonds reacted to a weaker-than-expected report on regional business activity from the Philadelphia Federal Reserve.
While the data did not eliminate market tension over the chances of another interest rate increase, analysts said it did offer at least some evidence that economic growth might be moderating.
"The Philly Fed numbers show some signs of slowdown in the manufacturing sector, and that's a good thing," said Bill Meehan, analyst at Prudential Securities.

In late New York trading, the dollar fell to 1.7238 German marks from 1.7285 marks late Wednesday after Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the German central bank does not want the German currency to weaken further. The dollar rose to 125.98 Japanese yen from 125.75 yen.
Wheat prices soared as export prospects improved after the European Union said it would suspend its weekly sales tenders.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat for May delivery soared the allowable 20-cent per bushel daily limit on the news and closed at $4.25-1/4, up 18-1/2 cents and at the highest closing price since Sept. 3.

Booming pork exports, especially to Japan, pushed prices higher at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange. Pork bellies for May delivery closed up the allowable 3.00 cent a pound daily limit at 87.55 cents and the June lean hog contract soared the daily 2 cent a pound limit to close at 85.45 cents.

At the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee futures closed higher following Tuesday's surprising report of smaller-than-expected warehouse coffee stocks in the United States. Coffee for May delivery closed at 209.80 cents, up 1.75 cents.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index ended 4.3 points higher at 4,298.9. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average rose 62.21 points, or 0.35 percent, to close at 18,093.41.
